slides.title: Four sides, or more?
slides.kicker: Six strange figures question the obvious definition
bullets: Informally, a quadrilateral is a figure with four straight sides, like ABCD.
The book tests us with six odd figures: NOPE, SILY, DART, CUTS, OPENS and BENT.
If we say no to any of them, our definition must explain exactly why it is excluded.
slides.note: Simple shabd, strict definition — that is real maths.

slides.title: Triangles teach first
slides.kicker: Define a triangle before touching quadrilaterals
bullets: Triangle ABC is the set of points on the three segments AB, BC and CA, provided A, B, C are not collinear.
If the three points sit on one line, the segments collapse into a single line segment, not a triangle.
When A, B, C are non-collinear, they are the vertices and AB, BC, CA are the sides.

slides.title: No three in line
slides.kicker: Rule one removes NOPE and SILY
bullets: First requirement: no three vertices of a quadrilateral may be collinear.
If three vertices sit on one line, the two adjacent sides formed by them lie along that same line.
This creates a triangle-like figure such as NOPE, or a figure with overlapping sides like SILY.

items: Take 4 points A, B, C, D

slides.title: Stay in one plane
slides.kicker: Rule two rejects the figure BENT
bullets: Second requirement: all four vertices must lie in the same plane.
Four-sided figures like BENT are called non-planar quadrilaterals.
This chapter studies only planar quadrilaterals, except in a few exercises.

right.title: Non-planar, like BENT
items: kept aside, a few exercises only

slides.title: Sides must not cross
slides.kicker: Rule three handles CUTS and OPENS
bullets: Ordinarily CUTS is not considered a quadrilateral; if we allow such figures, we call them self-intersecting quadrilaterals.
The fix: all the points of the quadrilateral, other than the vertices, must lie on exactly one side.
This single condition rules out crossing figures like CUTS and tricky ones like OPENS.

items: Take four points A, B, C, D
Other points on exactly one side

slides.note: Three checks ho gaye — now ABCD truly earns its name.

slides.title: The parallelogram family
slides.kicker: Opposite sides parallel: rhombus, rectangle, square
bullets: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel, as studied in Grade 8.
Rhombuses, rectangles and squares are all included in the family.
Parallelograms form a very important and widely used class of quadrilaterals.

slides.title: Theorem 1: three gifts
slides.kicker: Proved last year, reused all chapter
bullets: In a parallelogram, the opposite sides are equal.
The opposite angles are equal too.
And the diagonals bisect each other — three properties in one theorem.

slides.title: Proving sides equal
slides.kicker: One diagonal, one ASA test
bullets: In parallelogram ABCD, the diagonal AC is a transversal for AB parallel DC and also for AD parallel BC.
So triangle ACD is congruent to triangle CAB by the ASA test.
Matching parts give AB = DC and AD = BC — the opposite sides are equal.

items: AC is a transversal of both parallel pairs

slides.title: Angles from parallels
slides.kicker: Adjacent angles team up to 180 degrees
bullets: BC is parallel to AD with AB as transversal, so angle A plus angle B is 180 degrees.
They are interior angles on the same side of the transversal.
Any two adjacent angles add to 180 degrees, and algebra gives angle A = angle C and angle B = angle D.

slides.title: Converses become tests
slides.kicker: Flip Theorem 1 to detect parallelograms
bullets: Write each property in if-then form, then flip it: if the opposite sides are equal, is it a parallelogram?
The book shows that all three converse statements are true.
So there are alternate tests: equal opposite sides, equal opposite angles, or diagonals that bisect each other.

right.title: Converse direction
items: given equal sides, angles or bisecting diagonals

slides.note: Ulta karke dekho — each converse is a ready-made test.

slides.title: Parallelograms at work
slides.kicker: From forces to steam engines
bullets: In physics, a fundamental law uses parallelograms to combine physical quantities like forces, coming in a later year.
Mechanical linkages use them too, such as the parallel motion linkage discovered by James Watt.
Watt's linkage formed an important part of his steam engine.

slides.title: The clever pantograph
slides.kicker: A parallelogram that copies drawings
bullets: A pantograph is a parallelogram-based device that can make exact scaled copies of a drawing.
Watt's parallel motion design used the concept behind the pantograph.
The book suggests searching the internet for a pantograph video — it is ingenious!

slides.title: Cut a triangle into four
slides.kicker: An exploration with scissors and folding
bullets: Draw and cut out two copies of the same triangle; keep one intact for comparison.
On the other, mark the midpoint of each side — fold the paper to join two vertices at a time.
Draw the triangle made by the three midpoints and cut along these lines: you get four smaller triangles.

items: Draw two copies of a triangle

slides.title: All four are congruent
slides.kicker: The pattern the paper pieces reveal
bullets: The four smaller triangles appear to be congruent to each other.
Each one also seems to be a smaller copy of the original triangle.
Verify that this pattern holds for triangles of other shapes.

slides.title: One segment at a time
slides.kicker: Breaking a hard proof into steps
bullets: Try to prove the four triangles congruent directly and no congruence test applies, because many quantities are unknown.
The book's idea: too many new things at once — three new points and three new segments — so break it into steps.
For one segment joining two midpoints, the cut-outs suggest it is parallel to the unused third side and half as long.
slides.note: Bade kaam ko chhote steps mein todo.

slides.title: Tilings everywhere
slides.kicker: Mosaics, Escher and honeycombs
bullets: Tiling the plane with one shape or many leads to beautiful pictures.
They occur in mosaics of several ancient civilizations and in artwork like that of M.C. Escher.
Nature tiles too, for example a honeycomb, and so do decorative patterns of daily life.

slides.title: Any 4-gon can tile
slides.kicker: Meet the irregular quadrilateral SOME
bullets: The plane can be tiled with any given 4-gon, not just a parallelogram as at the beginning of the chapter.
Trace SOME on paper with its four angles labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 — remember they add up to 360 degrees.
Cut out 15 identical copies and start experimenting.

slides.title: The 360 degree secret
slides.kicker: Four copies hug one point
bullets: At any vertex of a tiling, the angles made by consecutive lines around it must total 360 degrees.
Idea: take 4 copies of SOME and fit them around a common point so each angle is used once as you go around.
There are multiple ways of doing this — continue fitting further copies and the plane gets tiled.

slides.title: Method 1: half-turn
slides.kicker: Rotate a copy about the edge midpoint
bullets: Start with two copies of SOME, one exactly above the other.
Rotate the top copy by 180 degrees around the midpoint of OM: the rotated copy aligns with the original perfectly along the shared edge OM.
Repeat this at each edge of every copy you add — the first step adds 4 copies around the starting copy, and the second step adds more.

slides.title: Describe it, prove it
slides.kicker: Experiment first, then justify
bullets: This section focuses on experimental verification of the tiling methods.
Challenge one: describe the procedure so precisely that someone can draw the tiling on their own.
Challenge two: justify why your procedure works — you are encouraged to prove it yourself.
slides.note: Pehle haath se try karo, phir proof.

quiz.q: Which of the book's six tricky figures is a non-planar quadrilateral?
quiz.why: BENT's four vertices do not all lie in one plane; NOPE and CUTS fail other checks.

quiz.q: Which requirement rules out SILY, which has overlapping sides?
options: All four vertices must lie in one plane
No three vertices may be collinear
quiz.why: Three collinear vertices force the two adjacent sides onto the same line, as in SILY.

quiz.q: To exclude self-intersecting figures like CUTS, the book requires that
options: each angle is less than 180 degrees
every point other than the vertices lies on exactly one side
quiz.why: That single condition keeps all non-vertex points on one side, ruling out crossing figures.

quiz.q: The diagonals of a parallelogram always
quiz.why: Theorem 1(c): the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

quiz.q: In the proof of Theorem 1(a), triangle ACD is congruent to triangle CAB by which test?
quiz.why: With AC as transversal of the parallel sides, ASA applies, giving AB = DC and AD = BC.

quiz.q: In parallelogram ABCD, angle A is 70 degrees. What is angle C?
quiz.why: Adjacent angles add to 180 degrees, and then algebra shows opposite angles are equal.

options: The triangles are not really congruent
Congruence tests work only for right triangles
Many quantities are unknown, so no congruence test applies
The midpoints cannot be found exactly
quiz.why: Too many new points and segments at once; the fix is to study one segment at a time.

quiz.q: A honeycomb is the book's example of tiling
quiz.why: Tilings occur in nature, for example a honeycomb, alongside mosaics and Escher's art.

options: Each angle of SOME is 90 degrees
Opposite angles of SOME are equal
All sides of SOME are equal
Its four angles add up to 360 degrees
quiz.why: Angles around a tiling vertex total 360 degrees, so each of the four angles is used once.

options: the copies overlap only at vertex O
the rotated copy aligns perfectly along the shared edge OM
the copy shrinks to half its size
the copies no longer touch each other
quiz.why: The half-turn about the edge midpoint makes the two copies align exactly along OM.

examples.title: Diagonals decide the parallelogram
examples.problem: A quadrilateral has vertices A(1, 1), B(5, 2), C(6, 6) and D(2, 5). Use the diagonal test to decide whether ABCD is a parallelogram.
steps: Use the converse of Theorem 1(c): if the diagonals bisect each other, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
The two midpoints coincide, so each diagonal cuts the other into two equal parts.
examples.answer: Both diagonals share the midpoint (3.5, 3.5), so they bisect each other and ABCD is a parallelogram.

examples.title: Angle chase in a parallelogram
examples.problem: In parallelogram ABCD, angle A is 70 degrees. Find angles B, C and D.
steps: Adjacent angles are interior angles on the same side of a transversal between parallel sides, so they add to 180 degrees.
Opposite angles are equal: angle C = angle A = 70 degrees and angle D = angle B = 110 degrees.
Check the total: 70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360 degrees, as the four angles of a quadrilateral must.
examples.answer: Angle B = 110 degrees, angle C = 70 degrees and angle D = 110 degrees.

examples.title: The midpoint cut-up, with numbers
examples.problem: A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. Its three midpoints are joined and the paper is cut along these segments. How many pieces appear and what are their side lengths?
steps: Joining the three midpoints and cutting gives four smaller triangles.
Each midpoint halves its side, so the triangle formed by the midpoints has sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm.
Each of the four small triangles is a smaller copy of the original, so every piece has sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm.
The four small triangles are congruent to each other, each at half the scale of the original triangle.
examples.answer: Four congruent triangles, each with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm — half-size copies of the original.

examples.title: Do four copies fit around a point?
examples.problem: An irregular 4-gon SOME has angles 95, 85, 105 and 75 degrees. Can four copies of SOME fit around one point the way Section 12.4 suggests?
steps: Around any vertex of a tiling, the angles made by consecutive lines must total 360 degrees.
Add the four angles of SOME: 95 + 85 + 105 + 75 = 360 degrees.
Place four copies around a common point, using each angle exactly once as you go around.
The angles fill the full turn exactly, so the four copies fit with no gap left over.
examples.answer: Yes — the four angles sum to 360 degrees, so four copies fit around one point, each angle used once.
